p.seg: Honorable Shaoqing,
sometime ago you condescended [debased yourself CH] to send a letter

instructing me about my responsibilities to exercise due care when dealing with others ["about being careful in dealing with things ZL: 待人接物" responsibilities is not in the text and unnecessary in the translation CH]
and my duty to recommend worthy men and promote gentlemen for court service. [and about taking it to be my duty to recommend worthies and promote (suitable) gentlemen CH]
While your intention was utterly sincere,
it is as if you thought that I might not regard you as my teacher [it is as if you blame me for not using your words as those of a teacher CH]
but would instead treat your words as the advice of the common run of men. [but went along with the talk of the run of men.CH]
I would not dare behave in such a way. [But it isn't as if I would ever take the liberty to take this attitude. CH]
Although but a broken-down nag, [I may be a... but ...CH]
I have stood by and heeded my elders’ examples. [but I surely have been listening in on, in my time, on the received wisdom of the elders. (“侧闻：从旁闻知。李善注：“谦词也。” CH]
Now, however, I consider my body ruined and debased. [I feel my body is mutilated and I am reduced to filling a filthy job. CH]
Whenever I act, I meet reproach. [Whenever I take an initiative I get blamed for it CH]
Those I would benefit, I only harm. [where I wish to profit others, on the contrary I harm them. CH]
“So it is I stifle my grief and have no one to speak to.”2 [perhaps: and never talk about it to anyone CH]
A proverb asks, [As the proverb has it CH]
“On whose behalf would you act? [Who to act for? CH]
And who can be made to heed you?” [Whom to get to listen to this? CH]
After Zhongzi Qi died, [It appears that after... 余誠 《古文釋義》：子期先死，伯牙听说后毁琴 CH]
Boya never again played the lute.3
Why is that?
A gentleman will do his utmost for someone who appreciates him, [An educated person will (only) make himself useful for someone who appreciates him (用≠盡力) CH]
just as a woman will adorn herself for someone who delights in her.4 [is pleased with her. (說≠樂)
But in cases like mine, when the body has been mutilated beyond repair, [physical frame CH 大質 is stylistically marked]
things are different: even if the person possesses the fine qualities of Sui’s pearl or He’s jade, [then even if one harboured treasures like Sui's and He's, CH]
and conducts himself as well as Xu You or Boyi,
he can never achieve honor and glory. [one could never be recognised as illustrious CH]
He would only provoke ridicule and besmirch himself.5 [all this would enable one to do is to provoke ridicule and to bring humiliation upon oneself, that is all. CH]
I should have answered your letter, [Letters one should answer/letters should be answered: no explicit irrealis here CH]
but I was just at that time traveling toward the east with the emperor.6. [It so happened that... The point about contingency is important CH]

And then I was pressed with inconsequential business [賤≠小：vulgar business 贱 does not mean "inconsequential/unimportant" business. The lively aggressiveness of the writer's style is narratively important here. CH]

so that there were but a few days when we could have seen each another. [and on the times we met, were few and far between (I suspect this formulation of being colloquial and do not feel it would come very naturally to a forger. The fact that everybody reads 淺 as meaning 少 is interesting, but without 根據 this proves nothing. 待考) CH]

I was so busy that I did not have a single moment to express my feelings fully to you. [I was so awfully busy that I did not have a free moment to tell you all that is on my mind. (Feelings are not mentioned. I would not expect a forger to invent 竭指意, but that is just a subjective impression that needs to be discussed with more advanced connoisseurs ) CH]
But now, Shaoqing, you have been declared guilty of an unfathomably serious crime. [an absurd criminal accusation CH]
The weeks and months are passing by, [as decamerons and months pass CH]
and soon it will be the final month of winter.7 [we willl get to the 12th month (I think the full stop here is the wrong punctuation in this context.)]

I am once again compelled to accompany the emperor up to Yong [when I'm again pointlessly/for no good reason, in the entourage of the emperor, going to be on my way to Shangyong, (The nuance, if right, would be important evidence on how Sima Qian looked upon his duties. This passage makes me suspect that this is a fake passage. CH]
and fear that suddenly the unspeakable might befall you.
And were I ultimately unable to vent my frustration and resentment and make them known, [In such a case if I WOULD HAVE failed to let you, my dear colleague, 左右：尊称对方。 know ... CH]

then a spirit departing for the long journey would harbor boundless regret.8 8. Songs 196. Cf. Legge (1960), p. 335, and Karlgren (1950B), p. 145. [”then on the long journey after my death, my spirits would feel boundless personal regrets.“ I find this highly melodramatic touch (長逝者魂魄) suspiciously unlike Sima Qian's prose style, but must leave it to others to decide on this point. CH]
So allow me to sketch out my crude thoughts,

and please do not blame me for my prolonged failure to respond. [This parenthetic disruptive return to a different topic is decidedly informal and not literary in nature. I doubt that a forger would tend to put it in here. But a spontaneous letter writer might well come to think at this matter at this point and put it in. But all this is just speculation. CH]

I have heard ["I'm told". This is not hearsay, from the street! The writer enters here into a broad survey of current moralising topoi defining man's moral place in the world (Er holt weit aus!...) CH]
that self-cultivation is the storehouse of wisdom; [Wenxuan has 符 “proof" for 府 "storehouse".]
magnanimity, the beginning of humaneness; ["generosity" for 愛施 （ JL：施舍“） is right, and this is not the same as magnanimity "nobility of attitude". CH]
discernment, the mark of dutifulness; [taking from and giving (appropriately) to the people) ... 取予 is not an ability but a course of action (ZL has it right). CH]
shame, after disgrace the decisive factor in courage; [being ashamed of public disgrace... CH]

and the desire to leave a good name, the ultimate wellspring of good behavior.9 [making a name for oneself..." is simple and correct. There is no "desire in the text", nor is there any mention of "leaving" a good name. CH]
Only after a gentleman possesses these five virtues [these five things (行 is not a virtue!) ...CH]
can he be commended to his generation [can he find his place in this world (No passive possible after 可以！託 remains problematic. CH]
and listed in the ranks of the truly noble.

Thus, no disaster is more hateful than that springing from coveting advantage;10 10. The structure of this passage is reminiscent of Analects 2.3: “Lead the people with administrative injunctions and keep them orderly with penal law, and they will avoid punishments but will be without a sense of shame; lead them with excellence (de) and keep them orderly through observing ritual propriety (li ) and they will develop a sense of shame, and moreover, will order themselves.” [No disaster is more tragic than that which springs from one's seeking the best. 欲利 is crucially different from 貪圖私利 and 欲 is never “covet”. Footnote 10 does not help on the essential point of this.CH]
no sorrow more painful than a shattered spirit; [than that being heart-broken." 傷 is not adjectival CH]
no action more repugnant than dishonoring one’s forebears;
and no infamy greater than suffering castration.
A man left a remnant from a mutilating punishment
counts for nothing in others’ estimation. [is altogether beyond the pale CH]
Not only in one era has this been so.
This has always been the case.
In times past, when Lord Ling of Wei shared a chariot with Yong Qu,
Confucius left for Chen.11
When Shang Yang relied on the Eunuch Jing to win an audience with the Qin ruler,
Zhao Liang’s heart froze.12
And when the Han emperor had Zhao Tong ride with him in his carriage,
Yuan Si turned red with anger and dismay.13 [got visibly upset". [Yuan Si made a scene. He showed he was upset. There is no "red" colour, no "anger" and no "dismay" in 變色也. CH]
From antiquity, then, to consort with eunuchs has been a source of shame. [one has deemed castrates to be a disgrace. CH]
Even a man of mediocre talent [Any person of ordinary standing (talent is not here the issue) CH]
will always risk real damage to his qi when he comes into contact with a eunuch in the course of his business.14. [a castrate (the term is impolite)CH]
How much more so a gentleman with soaring aspirations!
The court may currently lack the right sort of men, [suitable candidates/talent CH]

but why do you think it would allow a remnant of knife and saw to recommend men of distinction in the empire? [But how would they charge a subject of physical punishment by knife and saw with recommending the MOST outstanding heroes under the sun (I have not found good examples of 令 meaning "allow to", and no mention of this meaning in 漢語大詞典. When I find one, I will change my mind. CH]
Thanks to my father’s position,

I have managed to serve for more than twenty years at the foot of the emperor’s chariot, [I have fearfully served... (this self-deprecatory cliché description is especially apposite in Sima Qian's case. Note that we are told that Sima Qian is asked to accompany the emperor on official missions. The flowery style is significant here: 待罪 “serve in fear of death") CH]
From this I have learned some things about myself: [On which basis I have been thinking to myself as follows: CH]
First,
I have been unable to demonstrate my loyal service or prove my trustworthiness,

nor have I gained a reputation as a fine talent and hard worker [nor have I been able to gain... (it is important to get the syntax right, but one notes that ZL also gets the syntax wrong. DeepSeek gets it mechanically right)CH]

such as would bind our illustrious ruler to me. [or to link up with an enlightened sovereign; (the clear subtle meaning of 結明主 here is captured perfectly by DeepSeek although DeepSeek misses out on the overall syntactic structure) CH]
Second, [Second:
I have been unable to remedy deficiencies in the administration, [In addition, I have been INCAPABLE of mopping up (administrative) leftovers and omissions,
making sure that the summonses duly go out to worthy men to take up office [ of recruiting the worthy and promoting the capable, (here again DeepSeek gets the semantics right, but not the syntax）CH]
and that those living in reclusion become famous. [and of bringing recognition to the cave hermits in the hills (the liveliness of this is stylistically significant) CH]
As for external threats, [As regards matters outside the court,]

I have failed to serve in the military ranks. [I am incapable of providing armed forces (Sima Qian was supposed to be useless as a soldier, I think. In any case 備 does not tend to mean "serve in". CH]
I have captured no forts and fought on no field. [of attacking cities or fighting open field battles CH]
I have gained no merit for beheading enemy generals and seizing enemy flags. [or of gaining merit for cutting down generals or capturing enemy banners CH]
Finally,

I have not been able to exert every effort and accumulate achievements, [I have been incapable of cumulative daily meritorious toils (this throws interesting light on Sima Qian's self-portraiture as an intellectual!) CH]

to obtain high office and an exalted position, [of obtaining an exalted position with a substantial endowment/emoluments (the endowment would have been important since Sima Qian did not come from a rich family.) CH]
so as to bring glory and imperial favor to my family and those I am in contact with.16 [so as to bring glorious imperial favour to my family and my associates. CH]
I have not succeeded in any one of these four endeavors. [Having got nowhere in any one of these four things. CH]
It should be obvious that in simply conforming to the expectations of others and seeking their approval, [then through getting accepted by flexible adaptation CH]
I have not been of the slightest utility to the court.17 [I would not have any short or long term contributions to make: CH]
In the past, [In those days (this is not about any vague distant past but a certain stage in his career) CH]

I was regularly placed among the lower officers [I was, in my time, sidelined as one of the lesser dignitaries (it is important that Sima Qian WAS a dignitary, but of a lower rank, not just an officer. CH
who participate in minor deliberations in the outer court.
I did not make use of that time to elicit a master plan for governing [to draw up any principles of governance (no eliciting here, I think) CH]
or to offer my best thinking. [AND to exhaust my intellectual potential. CH]

Today, with my ruined body, I am fit only to be a servant who sweeps and cleans, [...I have become a minion who sweeps and cleans (there is nothing said here about being fit for nothing more than this]
about rights and wrongs in an arrogant fashion, [and dispute on the exact rights and the wrongs of things CH
dwelling among the most despised. [among the chaff (note the style!) CH]
Were I now to lecture others [Were I now to cut a proud uplifted figure (the text has nothing about lecturing here) CH]
would that not insult the court [would I then not make light of the (dignity of) court CH]
and shame the gentlemen of our age? [(be obliged to) feel ashamed before (the construction is puzzling.)CH]
Alas!
Alas!
For one like me,
what is there still to say?
What is there still to say?
Moreover, the course of events is not easy to explain. [is not so easy to understand (未≠不）CH]

As a youth my behavior was unrestrained; [In my youth I carried unbridled talents; (it is not behaviour but talents that are focussed in this highly important self-characterisation. The use of 负 is subtle )CH]
as I grew up, I won no fine name in my hometown. [and as I grew older I never earned praise in my local neighbourhood. CH
Fortunately for me, our ruler, on account of my deceased father,
ordered me to offer my meager skills to the court [got me to get to (得）offer...CH]
and gave me leave to come and go in the royal presence.18. [and to have access to the royal circles (no permission mentioned: 使 does not have two meanings in the two phrases) CH]

But how can someone with a basin on his head ever look up to Heaven?19 The thrust of this metaphor seems to be that Sima Qian felt he could not serve the empero well with any personal encumbrances. As he goes on to argue, he neglected all personal connections in order to satisfy the emperor and gain his favor. But Nylan offers other readings,equally attested in early writings, in chapter 4 in this volume. [But I thought to myself that 'wearing a (kitchen) pan as I hat, how am I to gain a perspective on high Heaven?' (i.e. without cutting myself off from my lower social connections I cannot engage with the higher visions of governance at court. Don Qijote's helmet is helpful for understanding this phrase. ...).CH]
So I cut myself off from the recognition of associates [Therefore I cut off relations with my social acquaintances

and ignored my duties to my family. [neglected my business at home. (I am delighted to see that Deep Seek has already registered this important common meaning of 忘 that is so commonly overlooked by sinologists. CH]

Day and night I wore myself out thinking how best to use every meager talent that I have in service; [Day and night I obsessed about how to make the most complete use of my hopeless talent and energy. CH]
I strove to devote myself wholeheartedly to my official duties, [I devoted myself (this is straighforward: no need for any explicit striving) CH]

the better to draw close to our ruler20 and gain his favor. 20 Nylan argues that this unusual expression (qinmei) sometimes describes a woman currying favor with her lover (see p. 75 in this volume). Li believes the associations of the word meican range from positive to negative (see p. 104 in this volume).
But in the course of acting so, I made a big mistake, and it was not to be. [But in the event I had it all completely wrong: (the punctuation here is crucial!!! CH]
Now, Li Ling and I had served together in the palace, [I had been stationed together with Li Ling (in the official quarters) by the Palace Gates. CH]

but we were never on particularly close terms.21 For Li Ling, the young general whom Sima Qian defended before the emperor, see Loewe2000, 224–25. Li Ling as Shizhong (Palace Officer) and Sima Qian as Taishi Ling (Director of Archives) both had the privilege of entering the palace gate. [but originally we were by no means on particularly close terms. (非 is not “never”， and 素 “basically” needs to be translated because it expresses an important nuance. CH]

As our inclinations ran along different paths, [Our prefences went different ways (I would prefer to say, but this makes no real difference, like probably quite a few of my other spontaneous alternative suggestions) CH
we had neither shared a single cup of wine nor formed a lively friendship. [we have never gathered for a cup of ale or any festive friendly gatherings. CH]

Observing his behavior, however, I considered him to be a gentleman of unusual ability. [And yet, on the basis of (distantly) observation, found his personality naturally outstanding. (the concept of 为人 is ancient, and already then inportant.)CH]
He was filial in serving his parents,
trustworthy in dealings with peers,
incorruptible in handling money,
fair in giving and taking,
deferential in maintaining the proper hierarchies,

and attentive and modest in yielding to others. [and humbly polite and sensitive to inferiors. (The respect for inferiors is an important feature here. (For six lines the author becomes numbingly conventional, and this is important, because this appreciation is not one of subtle personal friendship but of very conventional traditionalistic moral approval. The style matters greatly here. CH]

He always considered how best to meet any emergency that besets the ruling house, [he was constantly concerned to risk his life and indeed to die in defense against emergencies threatening the state. (不顧身 is crucial and must be focussed.) CH]
In view of all his previous accomplishments, [His basic cultivated and accumulated accomplishments were such CH]
I deemed him a gentleman of quality fully able to serve the realm. [that I deemed him to have the manner of a Hero of the State. (國士之風 needs focussed translation.CH]

For it is truly remarkable when a subject resolves to go out to face ten thousand deaths without the slightest regard for his own life [Now when a public servant come up with a plan that risks myriad deaths without any thought of personal survival CH]
or rushes forward to help out in any disaster that befalls the realm! [and rushes forth to help against any threat to the ruling duke's realm CH]
But now, in the course of discharging his duties, he made one mistake, [but when now, discharging his duty he got one single thing wrong, CH]

and court officials, who thought only of saving their skins and preserving their wives and children, stepped forward to exaggerate his shortcomings! [and the public servants, then, thinking of nothing but saving their own skins and those of their wives and children, followed this up and connived so as to malign the man's (general) inferiority of character, (the specific nuance of 短 here is crucial for the line of thought here) CH]
This truly made me sick at heart! [then, I sincerely felt personal sympathy for the man.]
Moreover, Li Ling led fewer than five thousand foot soldiers [Quite apart from all this ... CH]
and marched deep into the lands defended by nomads on horseback.
He and his men reached all the way to the Khan’s court, [stepping with his feet right into the (Hu) king's court (it is important that the Khan is referred as "the king" here, and NOT as the Khan)CH]
dangling bait in the tiger’s mouth
and boldly challenging those invincible Xiongnu. [the powerful Hu-barbarians (of the north) CH]

Facing tens of thousands of enemy troops,22 22 Li Ling’s biography in Hanshu 54.2456 has yi 抑 (overpower) for yang 仰 (face, confront),which would lead to the translation “overpowering tens of thousands of enemy troops.” [facing up to an army of myriads (he was not just facing troops, but an army, and that army is of INNUMERABLE soldiers， not specifically tens of thousands) CH]
they engaged the Khan’s men in battle for over ten days, [in continuous battle CH]
killing more than the number of troops in their own army.
The enemy had no time to rescue the dying and succor the wounded;
their leaders, dressed in their felts and furs, all quaked with fear.

As a result, the Khan summoned his Worthy Kings of Right and Left.23 23 Worthy King of the Left and Worthy King of the Right were noble titles just below theKhan. [his 'Worthy Kings of Right and Left' (the scare quotes are semantically essential here. These kings are not here designated as really worthy.]
He enlisted anyone who could draw a bow [commoners who were competent in archery CH]

Li Ling’s army pushed for more than three hundred miles, fighting skirmishes every step of the way, [enaged in battles on all sides all along a vast front. (千里 is generic and not numerically precise.) CH]
until their arrows were gone and the road blocked. [but when their arrows had been used up, when they had no way out, CH]
No rescue forces arrived, [and no rescue forces arrived,
and the dead and wounded piled up.24. [the dead and wounded officers and men were piling up as it were. CH]
Even so, when Li Ling gave a call to rally his troops, [Even so, as soon as...CH
each and every soldier rose up. [all officers rose up to respond.CH]
With their faces covered in tears [with tears streaming over their bodies CH]
and awash with blood, their ranks advanced, [awash with blood they drank their tears CH]
thrusting forward their empty wooden bows [bending their empty crossbows CH]
to meet the enemies’ shining metal blades, [drawn sharp blades CH]
They then turned north to continue the struggle to the death against the enemy.
Before Li Ling had fallen into captivity, [(Li) Ling (the use of the personal name is possibly significant...)]
his messenger came to the Han court to report this, [to report (on the then state of the war) CH]

and all the court officers and princes raised their goblets to toast His Majesty’s health. [raised their goblets to offer up their felicitations (上 here does not refer to the emperor, of course, and this is crucial for the story.)CH]
A few days later
there came word of Li Ling’s defeat. [word spread on Ling's letter announcing his defeat (the messaging by letter and not by messanger is important)CH]
Because of this news, our ruler could no longer savor his food [at meals the emperor did not savour his delicacies on account of this,CH]
or enjoy granting audiences. [and during audiences was in a bad mood. CH]
The high-ranking ministers, in their grief and fear, [were worried and fearful, and CH]
did not know what to do. [did not know what to say in the open. CH]
observed the emperor so distraught and downcast, [saw how upset and distraught the emperor was (见≠观)

I really wanted to help him by giving him sincere advice, however stupid. In doing so, I failed to take into account my low status. [my utterly sincere inept considerations. (The addition of the last sentence at this point is actually quite interesting: why indeed did the author spontaneously put it in the sentence above and not here?)CH]

Considering that Li Ling had always denied himself the best foods so that he might share them with his fellow officers, [I was of opinion that Li Ling from the start was congenial with officers and dignitaries, 'avoiding to eat the best pieces and passing around what there was too little of', CH]
it was no mere coincidence that he had been able to get his men to fight to the death.25. [and was had a way of getting others to give their utmost, at the risk of their lives, CH]
Even the most famous generals of ancient times could not surpass him in this regard. [and in this he outdid even the most famous generals of antiquity. (the generals DID not surpass him) CH]
No matter that he had suffered defeat, [He may, in person, have come to suffer a defeat, CH]

one should ponder his intentions26 26 Here, the narrator alludes to a principle enshrined in Han law by which the intentions ofthe accused were to be taken into account in the sentencing process. [but that man (彼), when one observes his motivations, CH]

and, moreover, credit him with the desire to find the right way to repay the Han.27 27 This implies that even as a captive among the Xiongnu, Li Ling is biding his time, intendingto act to further Han interests. [did also intend, when the opportunity presented itself, to pay his debt to the Han.CH]
His situation had left him with no options, [Under the circumstances there was nothing he could do CH]
yet his merit, considering the enemy troops he smote,
should have sufficed to win him fame throughout the empire. [this merit surely deserved to make him famous everywhere under the sun CH]
I harbored a wish to explain all of this, [all this it was my desire to spell out CH]
but I found no way to do so. [but had so far found no way to do this. CH]
Just at that point, I was summoned into the imperial presence on a question, [But just at that point it so happened... (I'm delighted to DeepSeek basically agrees...)] CH
and I took the opportunity to speak of Li Ling’s achievements in these very terms, [to elaborate on Ling's merits
hoping thereby to broaden the ruler’s understanding of the situation [the emperor's ideas CH]
and block the resentful criticisms. [angry rhetoric CH]
I somehow could not fully explain what I meant, [I was not quite capable of make myself completely clear CH]
and our illustrious ruler did not entirely understand.
He thought that I was slandering the Ershi General, Li Guangli,
while making clever excuses for Li Ling,
so I was sent down, a condemned man, to the judges.
For all my sincere and steadfast loyalty,
I ultimately could not give a good account of my actions. [to the very end I was incapable of giving a plausible account of myself. CH]
In consequence, I was found guilty of deceiving the emperor, [and so, naturally, I was deemed to have mislead the emperor CH]
and finally the judges’ decision was upheld.28 [and ultimately one followed the magistrate's exposition (of the facts of the case).]
My family, being poor, [Coming from a poor family
had insufficient funds to purchase remission of my crime.29 [my funds were insufficient to buy a pardon. CH]
None of my acquaintances offered to save me, [came to my rescue CH]

and none of my close associates put in a single word on my behalf.30 30The judicial process described here and in the sentences that follow is a bit murky. It seemsfrom other recorded cases that the crime of “deceiving the emperor” was a capital crime(see, e.g., Hanshu 6.187). The remission of a punishment through payment of money in theHan is well attested. Hanshu 6.206, for example, relates that in 95 bce, “they solicited thosewho had committed capital crimes to present a remission of 500,000 cash to reduce theirdeath sentence by one level.” Sima Qian’s castration (instead of execution) might have beenthe result of his petition for a commuted sentence. There were precedents for this reductionif the condemned so “desired” (Hanshu 5.147, 59.2650). Zhang Dake (1994) believesthat such reductions of sentence were fairly rare, however, and suggests that Emperor Wu“never had any intention to put Sima Qian to death” (124). The phrase “none of my closeassociates” may also mean “none among those close to the emperor.” [and my colleagues and closest relations did not utter a word (in my support).CH]

A body is not made of wood or stone! [I'm not made of wood and stone, (This narratively parenthetic remark is, of course an intensely personal outburs, like a sigh of self-pity. It is a pleasure to see that DeepSeek remembered this important reading of 身 "I, personally". )]
With only the officers of the law for company, [and all alone, with only ... CH]
I was kept in confinement deep within the prison walls. [deep down in the dark prison, CH]
To whom could I voice my grievances? [to whom could I... CH]
This is something that you, Shaoqing, have seen for yourself. [This, Shaoqing, is what you saw with your own eyes. CH]

Were my actions not as I have written? [Was not my conduct as I've just said? (This communicative appeal comes far too late, and is a very lively spontaneous feature that I find unlikely to have been invented by a deliberate forger: no need to attribute this to the famous Sima Qian, I would have thought, for a forger. The author comes to think of it here, and in spontaneous real time composition, he puts these parenthetic lines in here, where they do not really belong.CH]
Once Li Ling had surrendered, [When Li Ling had surrendered ALIVE. (DeepSeek would not miss this one.)CH]
and thus ruined his family’s good name,
I, too, was thrust into the Silkworm Chamber,31 [then I, in turn, was shoved into the silkworm prison chamber (for castration) CH]

becoming irrevocably the laughingstock of the empire.32 32 32 Alternatively, reading zhong 重 as chong, “both of us became the laughingstock of theempire.” [and doubly I became the laughingstock of all the world." （Firstly because I defended Li Ling， secondly because I got castrated. I am suprised that DeepSeek has something like my reading.) CH]
So tragic!
So very tragic!

It is not easy to explain this sequence of events to vulgar men. [These matters are not so easy to explain in every detail to ordinary people. (This authorial reference to possible readership is striking. One wonders where this first emerges in ancient Chinese literature.) CH]

My late father’s merit was not on a par with those dignitaries with broken tallies or vermillion prescripts.33 33 The first Han emperor “broke tallies with meritorious officials to swear vows [of goodfaith]” and used “vermilion writing on metal contracts” (danshu tieqi) to absolve theirdescendants of possible prosecution (Hanshu 1B.81). [It is not as if (非) my rather had the kind of merits that are rewarded with broken tallies and vermillion letters of appointment: CH]

Men of letters, archivists, astronomers, and calendrical experts34 are classed with the diviners and invocators. 34 These figures command the kinds of expertise associated with the Director of Archives. [...are close in rank to somewhere between diviners and invocators of the dead CH]
In fact, these men the ruler toys with [are inherently the emperor's playthings: CH]
and patronizes in the same way as entertainers. [he maintains them like mere minstrels CH]
They are held in disdain even by the common run of men. [who are held in low esteem even by the common folk. CH]
Had I bowed to the law and accepted the death penalty, [accepted execution CH]
